catalog_quote: Ma Manda has a quantity- and quality-sensitive, left-headed stress system. Stress is not contrastive, but it is not entirely predictable either. The preference is for word-initial stress, though stress can occur on any syllable, depending on syllable weight. The phonological foot is a moraic trochee. This means that it is composed of a sequence of two light syllables, the first of which is stressed (ĹL), or one heavy syllable (H́). [p. 70] ... Ma Manda is an unbounded stress-accent language. ... Stress in MM is attracted to the first syllable, but if a “heavier” syllable is further to the right, then stress is often attracted to that syllable instead. [p. 72] ... Both vowel quality (quality-sensitivity) and coda consonants (quantity-sensitivity) contribute to a syllable’s weight in Ma Manda. new_statements.rule_in_words: Words are parsed left-to-right into moraic trochees and the leftmost foot carries primary stress, so the default is word-initial stress (two light syllables: ĹL); but syllable weight — a coda consonant (quantity) or a more open vowel, a > e o > ə > i u > ɨ (quality) — can pull stress rightward onto a heavier second (occasionally third) syllable, making the system 'unbounded'. Stress is not contrastive.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Author says words 'generally' have secondary stresses on alternating syllables/feet after the primary (e.g. [qó.bɨ.sè], [də́.bu.gùm]; (L̀L)(H́) [qù.su.wə́t]), all subordinated to the leftmost stress, but 'it is debatable whether there is any reliable distinction between primary and secondary stresses' and acoustic confirmation is left for future research (pp. 72, 74-75, 78).
new_statements.exceptions: 'not entirely predictable': lexical idiosyncrasies (baagût [ba.gɨ́t] vs laamut [lá.mut], p. 73); variability of some words in isolation (e.g. /təndon/ 'night', p. 75); phonetic cues do not converge ('split-cue' system, Gordon 2011, p. 71); high vowels seldom attract stress; postpositional enclitics tend not to attract stress; suffixes shift stress only if heavier than the root syllables (p. 75).
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is about the phonological word (§6.1, §7.1); at phrase level (§6.3, p. 78) the leftmost word stress in the phrase receives the highest prominence and the phrasal pitch accent, later stresses subordinated. Examples are isolation/citation forms; author notes isolation-form variability.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Ma Manda (ISO skc, glottocode sauk1252; Glottolog name 'Sauk'), spoken in the Erap (Finisterre) area of Morobe Province; the thesis treats the language as a whole (author abbreviates MM), no separate dialect restriction stated in the prosody chapter.

new_statements.relation_note: Word-for-word the same key paragraph as the existing_statement from Pennington 2016 (PhD thesis §6.1 p. 70); this e-book is the 2013 MA thesis from which the 2016 chapter descends. It adds an explicit not-tonal statement (p. 75), the full vowel-weight hierarchy, the unbounded-system characterization, the split-cue remark, secondary-stress alternation, the clitic/suffix behaviour and the (23f) counterexample. Catalog record itself has an empty rule field; this source fills it as weight-sensitive with initial default.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default stress on the first syllable; a heavier syllable to the right (closed syllable, or a more open/sonorous vowel by the hierarchy a > e o > ə > i u > ɨ) pulls primary stress onto itself, so stress can land on any syllable. The foot is a moraic trochee; the system is unbounded (p. 79). Stress is non-contrastive but not fully predictable; the language is explicitly not tonal (p. 75: 'though Ma Manda uses pitch—among other indicators—to manifest stress.. it is not a tonal language'). Phonetic cues (pitch, intensity, duration) do not converge ('split-cue' system, p. 77); §6.3 p. 89: 'Ma Manda is not a prototypical stress-accent language.'
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 79: 'It does seem that, generally, Ma Manda words have secondary stresses'; pp. 83-84, examples (25a-f): in trisyllables 'The first syllable has primary stress, while the third syllable has secondary stress—though it is debatable whether there is any reliable distinction between primary and secondary stresses'; §6.3 p. 89: 'Secondary stress is assigned in alternate syllables outward from the primary stress, though it is debatable whether the notion of secondary stress is applicable to Ma Manda. Iterativity cannot as yet be proven..'
new_statements.exceptions: p. 81 (23f) /lamut/ [lá.mut] 'poison': closed second syllable does not attract stress, 'which contradicts the pattern'; p. 84: variability of placement in isolation (e.g. /təndon/ 'night'), 'perhaps moving toward—or perhaps away from—a pitch accent system'; p. 84: 'the stress system appears to be consistent across different word classes. The only exception to this is postpositional enclitics which tend not to attract stress. Nominal and verbal suffixes do not cause stress to move unless they have a heavier syllable than the noun or verb root'; p. 83: schwa ranked above high vowels, contrary to Kenstowicz/de Lacy/Parker sonority rankings.
new_statements.identity_note: Pennington 2014 describes the dialect spoken in and around the villages of Saut and Lemang (p. 7, PDF 25), chosen for being farther from the road; fieldwork six months in Saut 2009-2012. He notes the Ethnologue name 'Sauk' was unknown to speakers and replaced by 'Ma Manda' (p. 15). Same variety as the 2016 thesis.
